quiz.question: Which OSI layer is primarily responsible for logical addressing and routing?
quiz.explanation: Layer 3 (the Network layer) handles logical addressing (IPv4, IPv6) and inter-network routing, allowing routers to forward packets across distinct network segments.

quiz.question: What is a MAC address primarily used for?
options: Identifying a local-link interface for frame delivery
quiz.explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit link-layer hardware identifier used by Ethernet and Wi-Fi to deliver frames locally across a single broadcast segment or switch.

quiz.question: What does TCP provide to an application?
quiz.explanation: TCP provides a connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream through sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow/congestion control.

quiz.question: Which statement about UDP is correct?
options: It always uses lower latency than TCP
It has no built-in delivery or ordering guarantee
It can only carry DNS queries
quiz.explanation: UDP is a connectionless, lightweight datagram protocol that does not provide built-in retransmissions, acknowledgments, or sequence ordering.

quiz.question: Which DNS record type associates a name with IPv4 address data?
quiz.explanation: An 'A' (Address) record maps a fully qualified domain name (FQDN) to a 32-bit IPv4 address. 'AAAA' maps to a 128-bit IPv6 address.

quiz.question: What does a DNS record's TTL primarily influence?
options: How long a response may be cached
The number of TCP ports available
quiz.explanation: TTL (Time to Live) in DNS specifies the number of seconds a recursive resolver or client is permitted to cache the DNS record before re-querying the authoritative nameserver.

quiz.question: What does HTTPS use to protect HTTP communication in transit?
quiz.explanation: HTTPS encapsulates HTTP application traffic inside a Transport Layer Security (TLS) cryptographic session (currently TLS 1.3), providing confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication.

quiz.question: How many total IPv4 addresses are in a conventional /26 prefix?
quiz.explanation: A /26 prefix leaves 32 - 26 = 6 host bits. 2^6 = 64 total addresses (with 62 conventionally usable host addresses after subtracting network and broadcast).

quiz.question: What does an HTTP 403 response generally indicate?
options: The server has no IP address
quiz.explanation: An HTTP 403 Forbidden status indicates the server understood the request and authenticated identity, but refuses to fulfill it because permissions or authorization policies were not met.

quiz.question: Which is a correct interpretation of a successful ping?
options: All application security controls are effective
ICMP reachability succeeded for that test
quiz.explanation: A successful ping only proves that ICMP Echo Request and Reply succeeded at the network layer (L3). It does NOT verify that TCP, TLS, web services, or application security controls are operational.

scenarios.title: Fault A: Client Cannot Reach Local Gateway
scenarios.symptom: Student laptop cannot access intranet portal or ping default gateway 192.168.20.1.
scenarios.cliOutput:
PS C:\Users\Student> ipconfig /all
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.20.140
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.192
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.20.1

PS C:\Users\Student> ping 192.168.20.1
Pinging 192.168.20.1 with 32 bytes of data:
Destination host unreachable.
scenarios.analysis: SUBNET MISMATCH: With /26 (mask 255.255.255.192), host 192.168.20.140 sits in subnet 192.168.20.128/26 (range .129 - .190). The configured gateway 192.168.20.1 sits in subnet 192.168.20.0/26. The client assumes the gateway is on its local broadcast domain, but ARP cannot cross subnet boundaries.
scenarios.fix: Configure the gateway IP to 192.168.20.129, or reassign the student host to 192.168.20.25 within Subnet 1.

scenarios.title: Fault B: DNS Resolution Succeeds, But HTTP 403 Forbidden
scenarios.symptom: Learner attempts to download their interview report, but receives an HTTP 403 status code.
scenarios.cliOutput:
PS C:\Users\Student> nslookup learn.example.com
Server:  1.1.1.1
Address: 1.1.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    learn.example.com
Address: 104.21.58.192

PS C:\Users\Student> curl -I https://learn.example.com/api/reports/1048
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
X-Security-Alert: Unauthorized access attempt
scenarios.analysis: APPLICATION AUTHORIZATION FAILURE: DNS resolution and TCP/TLS handshakes succeeded perfectly. The 403 Forbidden status indicates that the web server understood the request, but the client identity lacks authorization to view Report #1048.
scenarios.fix: Verify user session permissions; ensure the requesting student owns the record or has been granted academic mentor permissions on the server.

scenarios.title: Fault C: TLS Certificate Domain Name Mismatch
scenarios.symptom: Browser flags connection as dangerous; command line returns SSL peer certificate error.
scenarios.cliOutput:
PS C:\Users\Student> curl -I https://internal.learnsphere.org
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'internal.learnsphere.org'
More details here: https://curl.se/docs/sslcerts.html
scenarios.analysis: CERTIFICATE VALIDATION FAILURE: The TLS certificate presented by the server has Subject Alternative Name (SAN) configured only for 'api.learnsphere.org' and 'learnsphere.org', missing 'internal.learnsphere.org'.
scenarios.fix: Re-issue the TLS certificate via Let's Encrypt / DigiCert with 'internal.learnsphere.org' or '*.learnsphere.org' included in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extensions.

theorySections.title: What Truly Happens When You Open a Website? (https://example.com)
paragraphs: Visiting a website is not a single atomic operation. It is an orchestration of protocol handshakes, distributed lookups, encapsulation, and cryptographic verifications:
Client stub queries resolver to map FQDN to an IPv4/IPv6 address.
Packets routed via default gateway across Autonomous Systems.
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange establishes reliable stream state.
Server identity verified via X.509 cert; session keys derived.
Encrypted GET request; server returns status 200 and HTML payload.

theorySections.title: Lesson 1.1–1.4: Network Topologies, Components & Metrics
paragraphs: A computer network connects nodes (endpoints, switches, routers) via physical or wireless communication channels to exchange data according to shared protocols.
LAN: Local Area Network in single room or building (Ethernet/Wi-Fi). WAN: Wide Area Network spanning cities/continents. VPN: Encrypted logical tunnel traversing untrusted public networks.
Star: Central switch connecting all devices (predominant modern LAN). Mesh: Interconnected nodes offering redundant failover paths at higher complexity.
Topology dictates adversary lateral movement paths. Segmenting databases from internet-facing web servers limits compromise radius.
Data is chopped into independent packets routed dynamically across statistical multiplexing links, rather than reserving dedicated circuit lines.

theorySections.title: Lesson 2.1–2.4: Layering, Encapsulation & Packet Construction
paragraphs: Networking uses layered abstraction so hardware vendors, OS kernels, and application developers can innovate independently:

{` [Application Layer] [HTTP Payload / GET /index.html] | v (Add TCP Header: Src Port 54120, Dst Port 443, Seq #) [Transport Layer] [TCP Header | HTTP Payload] ==> "Segment" | v (Add IP Header: Src IP 192.168.1.25, Dst IP 104.21.58.192) [Network Layer] [IP Header | TCP Header | HTTP Payload] ==> "Packet" | v (Add Ethernet Header: Src MAC, Dst MAC, Type 0x0800 & FCS Trailer) [Data Link Layer] [Eth Header | IP Header | TCP Header | HTTP Payload | FCS] ==> "Frame" | v (Transmit on Physical Wire / Radio Frequency) [Physical Layer] 010111001010010101010101010101100010101001 ==> "Bits"`} Why Encapsulation Matters to Defenders Firewalls inspect Layer 3 and Layer 4 headers (IPs, Ports, TCP flags). Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) and proxies must inspect decapsulated Layer 7 payloads (HTTP URIs, JSON bodies). Furthermore, when traffic is encrypted via TLS, passive network eavesdroppers can see Layer 2, Layer 3, and Layer 4 headers, but the Layer 7 data remains entirely ciphertext.

theorySections.title: Lesson 3.1–3.7: MAC, IPv4 Subnetting, IPv6, ARP & NAT
paragraphs: A MAC address (48-bit hex e.g. 00:11:22:33:44:55) identifies an interface on the local wire. Routers rewrite the source and destination MAC addresses at every hop! IP addresses (32-bit IPv4 / 128-bit IPv6) provide end-to-end logical addressing and remain unchanged across intermediate routers (unless NAT is used).
• 127.0.0.0/8 - Loopback | 169.254.0.0/16 - APIPA Link-Local

Consider dividing 192.168.10.0/24 into four equal /26 subnets. A /26 prefix has 26 network bits and 6 host bits (32 - 26 = 6). Subnet mask: 255.255.255.192. Each subnet contains 2^6 = 64 total IP addresses:

Network Address Translation (NAT) modifies IP addresses in headers to solve IPv4 address exhaustion. While private IPs cannot be reached directly without stateful mapping, NAT does NOT inspect payloads, filter malicious inbound responses, or enforce authorization. Actual defense requires firewall access rules, identity validation, and endpoint hardening.

theorySections.title: Lesson 4.1–4.5: Reliable Streams, Sockets & Modern HTTP/3
paragraphs: Transport protocols demultiplex incoming packets to specific application processes using 16-bit port numbers (0 to 65535):
Client selects random Initial Sequence Number (ISN_c) and sets SYN flag (Synchronize).
Server acknowledges client ISN (Ack = ISN_c + 1) and sets its own ISN_s.
Client confirms server ISN (Ack = ISN_s + 1). Socket enters ESTABLISHED state.
Connection-oriented, reliable in-order byte stream. Features sliding window flow control and AIMD congestion control. Used by SSH (22), traditional HTTPS (443), and databases.
Connectionless, stateless, message-preserving. Zero retransmissions or packet ordering. Minimal header overhead (8 bytes). Used by DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), and NTP (123).
Runs over UDP with built-in TLS 1.3 encryption and congestion control. Eliminates Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking across independent streams, drastically accelerating mobile web access.

theorySections.title: Lesson 5.1–5.5: Hierarchy, Record Types, TTL & Security
paragraphs: DNS translates human-readable hostnames into network IP addresses. Critical security distinction: DNS only discovers where a service lives; it does NOT host the application or guarantee that the target is secure!

Because legacy DNS over UDP lacks cryptographic signatures, an attacker can flood a recursive resolver with forged responses. If accepted, the resolver redirects all legitimate users to an attacker-controlled server.

DNSSEC: Uses public-key cryptography to digitally sign DNS records, ensuring integrity and authenticity. DoH / DoT: Encrypts the query link between client and resolver, preventing local ISP eavesdropping.
